chief_complaint: sudden excruciating pain, redness, and swelling in big toe
hpi_details: A 32-year-old female presents to the clinic with sudden excruciating pain, redness, and swelling in big toe. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks she broke her toe by stubbing it in the dark or developed a severe bacterial infection from an ingrown toenail.
concerns: She is worried that the agony will keep her from putting on shoes and driving to work tomorrow.
expectations: She hopes to get an X-ray to check for a broken bone and a fast-acting pain relief injection so she can walk.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Gouty Arthritis evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Gouty Arthritis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes treating the flare with an NSAID or colchicine; continue established urate-lowering therapy, and initiation during a flare is acceptable when indicated with anti-inflammatory treatment, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Gouty Arthritis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Septic arthritis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Fever with joint swelling.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: sudden excruciating pain, redness, and swelling in big toe

A 32-year-old female presents to the clinic with sudden excruciating pain, redness, and swelling in big toe. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Acute Gouty Arthritis.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Acute Gouty Arthritis.
reference_soap.plan: Assess vital signs and examine for an effusion or cellulitis. Do not assume gout in a first or atypical acute monoarthritis: if septic arthritis is plausible, arrange urgent arthrocentesis with synovial cell count, Gram stain, culture, and crystal analysis. A clinician should select NSAID, colchicine, or glucocorticoid treatment after renal, gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, interaction, pregnancy, and infection-risk review. Continue established urate-lowering therapy unless the treating clinician advises otherwise; decisions to initiate long-term urate-lowering therapy require follow-up and individualized counseling.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Acute Gouty Arthritis
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Acute Gouty Arthritis

Implement evidence-based management plan: treat the flare with an NSAID or colchicine; continue established urate-lowering therapy, and initiate it during a flare when indicated with anti-inflammatory treatment

teaching.one_liner: Monosodium urate crystal deposition in a joint causing sudden excruciating pain, redness, and swelling, classically in the big toe.

must_ask.say: Which joint is affected — the big toe?
Did you eat a lot of meat or drink alcohol recently?

history.answer: My right big toe suddenly became swollen, red, and excruciatingly painful early yesterday morning, and it hurts so much I can barely touch it or walk.
It is only in my right big toe at the base joint. None of my other toes or joints on either foot or hand are swollen or painful.
It woke me up suddenly in the middle of the night yesterday, and the pain became intense within just a few hours.
It is a severe, throbbing pain, like my toe is burning or being crushed. On a scale from one to ten, it is easily a nine.
Yes, the base of my right big toe is puffy, bright red, and feels intensely hot to the touch.
I do not have any morning stiffness in my hands or other joints. My toe just throbs with constant, severe pain day and night.
Any movement or even the weight of a bedsheet touching my toe makes the pain unbearable. Resting and keeping my foot still helps slightly, but it still throbs.
I cannot put any weight on that foot at all. I had to limp in here stepping strictly on my heel and leaning on my husband.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or sweating.
No, I did not stub my toe, twist my foot, or suffer any injury, and I did not hear any popping sound.
No, I have never had pain, redness, or swelling like this in any joint before. This is the very first time.
I have felt unusually tired and worn out over the past few days, but I have not lost any weight.
No, I have not had any facial rash, flaky skin patches, mouth ulcers, hair loss, or dry eyes and mouth.
No, I do not have any lower back pain, morning spine stiffness, or pain in my heels.
No, I have not had any diarrhea, burning when I urinate, unusual discharge, or a recent sore throat.
Two nights ago, I went out for a heavy steak dinner and had two beers with colleagues. I do not take any water pills or diuretics.
No, I have never had joint injections, joint surgeries, or artificial joints, and I have never taken steroid medications.
I have been with my husband in a monogamous relationship for five years, and there are no new sexual partners.
I thought I must have stubbed and broken my toe during the night, or that an ingrown nail got badly infected.
I'm terrified that the pain will stay this terrible and I won't be able to put a shoe on or drive to work tomorrow.
I'm hoping for an X-ray to make sure it's not broken and a strong pain shot so I can actually walk out of here.
I have always been healthy and have never been diagnosed with high blood pressure, diabetes, or kidney disease.
No, I have never had any surgeries and I have never been admitted to a hospital.
I do not take any regular prescription medications. I tried taking an over-the-counter ibuprofen yesterday, but it did not help much.
No, I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or anything else.
No, I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only drink alcohol socially, usually one or two glasses of wine or beer on weekends.
I work as an accountant at an office, and I live in an apartment with my husband.
My paternal uncle has gout, but my parents are both healthy and there is no family history of rheumatoid arthritis or autoimmune diseases.
My last menstrual period was two weeks ago and my cycles are regular. We use barrier protection, and there is no possibility of pregnancy.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, heart rate 78 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, body temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert and visibly uncomfortable, guarding her right foot, but in no acute respiratory distress.
The right first metatarsophalangeal joint is markedly swollen, erythematous, hot to the touch, and exquisitely tender, with both active and passive motion severely restricted by pain.
No tophi on the ears, elbows, or finger joints, and no psoriatic plaques, malar rash, or petechiae.
Marked antalgic gait with complete refusal to bear weight on the right forefoot.
No peripheral edema in the calves, ankles, or opposite foot.
